title: What are JPA projections, how do interface, class/DTO, and dynamic projections differ, and how do they compare in performance?

s1_definition.profdef: Projections return only the columns you need instead of full managed entities. Spring Data supports interface-based projections (declare getters; Spring builds a proxy), class/DTO projections (a constructor expression or record populated directly), and dynamic projections (a generic method parameterized by the return type). Projections reduce data transfer, skip entity instantiation and dirty-check tracking, and can dramatically outperform loading full entities for read-heavy views.
s1_definition.analogy: Fetching a full entity is like National Bank of India pulling Rajesh's entire file — every page, photo, and history — just to read his balance. A projection is like asking only for a small index card with the two fields you actually need: name and balance. Interface projections are a card the clerk fills using a stencil (a proxy). DTO projections are a card you designed yourself with an exact slot for each field. Dynamic projections let you ask for different card layouts from the same request depending on what the caller wants.
s1_definition.oneliner: Projections fetch only the columns you need as lightweight read models, far cheaper than loading full entities.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Projections return only the columns you need instead of full managed entities. Spring Data supports interface-based projections (declare getters; Spring builds a proxy), class/DTO projections (a constructor expression or record populated directly), and dynamic projections (a generic method parameterized by the return type). Projections reduce data transfer, skip entity instantiation and dirty-check tracking, and can dramatically outperform loading full entities for read-heavy views.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Fetching a full entity is like National Bank of India pulling Rajesh's entire file — every page, photo, and history — just to read his balance. A projection is like asking only for a small index card with the two fields you actually need: name and balance. Interface projections are a card the clerk fills using a stencil (a proxy). DTO projections are a card you designed yourself with an exact slot for each field. Dynamic projections let you ask for different card layouts from the same request depending on what the caller wants.

**One line to remember:** Projections fetch only the columns you need as lightweight read models, far cheaper than loading full entities.

sections.s2_technical:
Interface-based projection: declare an interface with getters matching the properties you want, for example `interface AccountView { String getId(); BigDecimal getBalance(); }`, and a repository method `AccountView findViewById(String id)`. Spring generates a proxy backed by the selected columns. Closed projections (only direct getters) let Hibernate select just those columns; open projections (using @Value SpEL expressions) load the full entity first, losing the benefit.

Class/DTO projection: use a constructor expression in JPQL, `select new com.bank.dto.AccountDto(a.id, a.balance) from Account a`, or a Java record. Spring Data can also map a projection to a record automatically. This selects only the needed columns and produces an immutable, unmanaged object with no dirty tracking — the most predictable and often fastest option.

Dynamic projection: a method `<T> T findById(String id, Class<T> type)` lets the caller choose the shape at runtime, returning either a full entity, an interface view, or a DTO depending on the Class passed. One query method serves many read models.

Performance comparison: loading full entities is heaviest — it selects all columns, instantiates managed entities, and registers them for dirty checking. Closed interface and DTO projections are lightest because the SQL selects only the projected columns and the results are not managed. Open interface projections are slow because they fetch the whole entity then compute. For large result sets and read-only endpoints, DTO or closed interface projections cut both database I/O and heap pressure significantly.

Senior nuances: projections avoid the overhead of the persistence context, so they are perfect under @Transactional(readOnly=true). Native queries can map to interface projections by column alias. For aggregations (SUM, COUNT grouped), DTO projections are the natural fit. Beware that nested projections for associations can reintroduce N+1 unless the query join-fetches.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — A dashboard lists 50,000 accounts showing only id and balance. Loading full Account entities with twenty columns each wastes memory and bandwidth. This is exactly a projection — select only id and balance.

Problem 2 — We want an immutable, strongly typed read model for an API response, not a managed entity. This is exactly a DTO/record projection.

Problem 3 — The same endpoint sometimes needs a summary view and sometimes the full entity, depending on a query flag. This is exactly a dynamic projection.

We will build an AccountRepository with interface, DTO, and dynamic projections and compare them.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Build
mvn clean package -DskipTests

# Run
java -jar target/projection-service-1.0.0.jar

# Lightweight dashboard (interface projection)
curl http://localhost:8080/api/v1/accounts/dashboard

# DTO API list
curl http://localhost:8080/api/v1/accounts/dto

# Dynamic — summary vs full
curl "http://localhost:8080/api/v1/accounts/SAV2001?summary=true"
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input: dashboard of all accounts; DTO list; dynamic fetch of SAV2001 (summary=true).

Step 1 — dashboard calls findAllProjectedBy. Because AccountView is a closed interface with only getId and getBalance, Hibernate generates `SELECT id, balance FROM accounts` — not all six columns. It returns proxies, no managed entities, no dirty tracking.

Step 2 — apiList calls findAllAsDto with a constructor expression. Hibernate generates `SELECT id, holder_name, balance FROM accounts` and constructs immutable AccountDto records directly. No persistence-context overhead.

Step 3 — getOne with summary=true calls the dynamic findById passing AccountDto.class, so Spring selects only the DTO's three columns and returns a record. With summary=false it passes Account.class and loads the full managed entity with all columns.

Step 4 — Comparing cost: the full-entity path selects six columns, instantiates a managed entity, and registers it for dirty checking; the projection paths select two or three columns and skip all persistence-context overhead, so for 50,000 rows they transfer far less data and allocate far less heap.

```
Hibernate: select a.id, a.balance from accounts a            (interface projection)
INFO  Dashboard loaded 2 projected rows (id+balance only)
Hibernate: select a.id, a.holder_name, a.balance from accounts a   (DTO)
Hibernate: select a.id, a.holder_name, a.balance from accounts a where a.id=?  (dynamic summary)
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Read request
    │
    ├─ INTERFACE PROJECTION (dashboard)
    │    findAllProjectedBy → SELECT id, balance → proxies (no managed state)
    │
    ├─ DTO PROJECTION (api)
    │    findAllAsDto → SELECT id, holder_name, balance → immutable records
    │
    └─ DYNAMIC PROJECTION (getOne)
         findById(id, AccountDto.class) → light (3 cols)
         findById(id, Account.class)    → full entity (6 cols, managed)
    ▼
  Response (lightweight vs full depending on need)

  Cost: full entity = all cols + instantiate + dirty-track (heavy)
        projection  = few cols + no persistence context (light)
```

```
  │ + API  │      │ cache       │      │ interface/DTO/dyn   │

  Projections + covering index → index-only scans, minimal I/O.
```

```
  ═══ LLD — Interface vs DTO vs Dynamic Projection ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns ──────────────────────────────────┐
  │ DTO/Value Object: immutable read model              │
  │ Strategy (dynamic): caller picks shape via Class<T> │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID ────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ I: small focused view interfaces (AccountView)      │
  │ O: add a new projection without touching entity     │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌───────────────────────────────┐
  │   <<interface>> AccountRepo   │
  │  + findAllProjectedBy():View  │ closed interface
  │  + findAllAsDto(): Dto        │ constructor expr
  │  + findById(id,Class<T>): T   │ dynamic
  └──────────────┬────────────────┘
                 ▼ used by
  ┌───────────────────────────────┐
  │       AccountReadService      │
  │  + dashboard() → List<View>   │
  │  + apiList()   → List<Dto>    │
  │  + getOne(id,summary)         │
  └───────────────────────────────┘

  ── Performance ranking (read heavy) ──
  DTO / closed interface  → fastest (few cols, unmanaged)
  full entity             → heaviest (all cols, managed, dirty-track)
  open interface (@Value) → slow (loads full entity first)

  ── Call Chain (dynamic summary) ──
  1. getOne(SAV2001, true) → findById(id, AccountDto.class)
  2.   SELECT id, holder_name, balance WHERE id=?
  3. return immutable AccountDto
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Projections let me return only the columns a read actually needs instead of loading full managed entities, which is a major win on read-heavy banking endpoints. There are three kinds. An interface projection is an interface with getters for the properties I want, and Spring builds a proxy over the selected columns; as long as it is a closed projection with only direct getters, Hibernate selects just those columns. A class or DTO projection uses a constructor expression in JPQL or a Java record, producing an immutable, unmanaged object populated directly from the selected columns. A dynamic projection is a generic method that takes the desired type as a Class parameter, so one repository method can return a full entity, an interface view, or a DTO depending on what the caller asks for.

On performance, loading full entities is the heaviest option because it selects every column, instantiates a managed entity, and registers it for dirty checking in the persistence context. Closed interface and DTO projections are the lightest because the generated SQL selects only the projected columns and the results are never managed, so there is no snapshot and no dirty tracking. The one trap is the open interface projection that uses SpEL expressions, because it loads the whole entity first and then computes, which throws away the benefit.

In our National Bank of India system, a dashboard listing fifty thousand accounts needs only id and balance, so I use a closed interface or DTO projection and the query becomes an index-only scan over a covering index, transferring a fraction of the data and allocating far less heap. API responses use immutable record DTOs so the read model is strongly typed and cannot accidentally be mutated and persisted. Where one endpoint must sometimes return a summary and sometimes the full entity, I use a dynamic projection so a single method serves both shapes.

The senior points I add are that projections pair perfectly with read-only transactions because they avoid persistence-context overhead entirely, that DTO projections are the natural fit for aggregations like grouped sums and counts, and that nested projections across associations can reintroduce the N+1 problem unless the underlying query join-fetches, so I design the query and the projection together rather than in isolation.

---

keyPoints: Full entity: loads everything, dirty checking overhead
Interface projection: proxy, loads only declared fields
DTO projection: direct JPQL constructor, no proxy — fastest
Always use projection for read-only screens — avoid full entity loading
